label: Dispatch No. 2
tagline: The radical possibility of leaving something well alone.

letter.title: Welcome to Fallow
letter.lead: This month tugs on two of the Seven Principles: Recovery and Permission.
body: I have never made a New Year’s resolution.
I’ve been asked, encouraged and pressurised into doing so, but I always decline.
Frankly, I’ve always thought the concept of “New Year Resolutions” was bollocks.
Not because I lack ambition. I’ve got plenty of that, be assured. And not because I don’t believe in change, because I’ve spent much of my life changing things, including myself, constantly.
But I’ve never understood why the arrival of January should constitute evidence that I need fixing.
Or why, if I want to change something, I can’t just do so on another day of the year.
And in England, where the January days are long, cold, grey and dark – why would I choose THIS particular month to eject comforts from my life in an attempt to be “better”.
Yet every year, without fail, on 1st January we’re invited to begin again.
New year. New goals. New habits. New body. New business. NEW YOU.
(The implication being that the old you has somehow failed to meet expectations. Objection, m’lady. I’m perfectly well-rounded and content as I am.)

So having survived the chaos of December, we arrive in January exhausted, overfed, financially depleted and slightly bewildered, only to be instructed to embark upon an ambitious programme of personal transformation.
Preferably involving green juice, a gym membership and a journal with gold lettering.
No, thank you.
So this January, by order of the Society, we’re doing something different.

In fact, we’re not doing anything at all. Feck all. Nada. Zilch. Minus zilch, if such a thing is possible. Join me in the Land of the Fallow and the Free, where we investigate the curious art of emptying our baskets and searching for empty space.
If you’re new here, welcome to We Are Unbecoming. If you’ve been with us since December, welcome back, and well done for surviving the overdose of mince pies.
Either way, welcome to Fallow.
letter.ps: P.S. To our Correspondents in Australia, currently basting gently in the height of summer: bear with us whilst you swan around in your bikinis. The winter in these pages isn’t always the one outside the window, so it still applies to y’all.

lastPage.sub: Not a resolution. Not an assignment.
lastPage.question: What would you allow to lie fallow if you didn’t have to explain, justify or promise what it might eventually become?
lines: You don’t have to answer it. You could simply let it accompany you for a little while. On a walk. In the bath. On the train. While waiting for the kettle to boil.
You might find something worth considering. Or you might not.
lastPage.small: There is no thirty-day plan. No downloadable tracker. No accountability partner. No instruction to reinvent yourself before February.

finalWord.title: Trust.
body: We spend so much of our lives trying to make things happen.
Planning. Pushing. Building. Fixing.
Becoming.
And sometimes, I accept, those are exactly the things we need to do. Life is life’ing, and we have to get on.
But I’ve often reflected on what kind of courage it is when we intentionally leave something unfinished.
To allow a question to remain unanswered, or let a difficult friendship fade away.
When we stop trying to extract a lesson from every difficult experience, or stop beating ourselves up for our part in it.
The courage to believe that our worth is not conditional upon our usefulness or our worthiness, especially if we’re looking for it to be validated by others.
To trust ourselves without needing to know what happens next.
This is your friendly reminder: fallow ground has already been turned over. It has done its work. It is allowed to lie there.
So this January, you’re invited not to begin.
Not to become or do or graft your way to any particular destination or goal.
Not to make a single promise about the person you’ll be twelve months from now.
You are allowed to be here. Just as you are.

I’m very glad you’re here. And the books need you, because they’re getting unbearable. The ones as yet unwritten are grumbling, but I’ve told them – not till February comes. Hold your horses. The Plough is on annual leave until further notice.
